# Opposite singular core nodes force a cap fraction at least 8/17

This is an ordinary planar theorem. It excludes hexagon type B in the
fixed-sector row-maximization reduction whenever all three cap fractions
are at most 128/279. It does not exclude type A or prove a mixed-integer
depth theorem. The argument only uses a relaxation of the type-B
feasibility inequalities, so it covers its boundary strata as well.

## 1. Geometric setup and theorem

Let K be a planar convex body containing zero in its interior. Use the
balanced normals (1,0), (0,1), (-1,-1), and write its cyclic ray endpoints
as

  P_0=(A,0), P_1=(0,B), P_2=(-t,t),
  P_3=(-a,0), P_4=(0,-b), P_5=(r,-r),

where all six radii are positive. Let W_i be the area in the sector
between P_i and P_(i+1), with indices modulo six. Suppose sectors
0,2,3,5 are exactly their core triangles, and the three endpoints
P_5,P_0,P_1 are collinear, as are P_2,P_3,P_4. These are precisely the
four core equalities and the two opposite singular singleton conditions
in hexagon type B. No condition on strictness of the two other sectors
or positive definiteness of their blocks is required below.

Let k=|K| and let q_1,q_2,q_3 be its areas in the three closed halfplanes
x>=0, y>=0, and x+y<=0, respectively. Then

  max(q_1,q_2,q_3) >= (8/17) k.                       (1)

In particular these hypotheses are incompatible with q_i/k<=128/279
for every i, since

  8/17-128/279=56/4743>0.                             (2)

For general balanced spanning normals, apply the invertible map whose
rows are the first two normals. All ordinary areas acquire one common
positive determinant factor, preserving (1), (2), the sector equalities,
and the collinearities. This is an ordinary geometric normalization,
not a claimed lattice-preserving change of mixed coordinates.

## 2. Exact six-sector data

The collinearities give

  A=Br/(B+r),             a=bt/(b+t).

Set

  x=W_1, y=W_4,
  P=Bt/2, Q=br/2, U=Br/2, V=bt/2,
  Z=(AB+at)/2.

All these numbers are positive. Core inclusion gives x>=P and y>=Q,
and their products satisfy UV=PQ. Summing the four fixed sectors and
the two remaining sectors gives exactly

  k=x+y+U+V,
  q_1=y+U,   q_3=y+V,   q_2=x+Z.                    (3)

For example, W_0+W_5=A(B+r)/2=U and
W_2+W_3=a(t+b)/2=V. This proves the first and third cap formulas;
the second uses W_0+W_2=Z. Boundaries have zero ordinary area.

Put xi=B/r>0 and p=P/Q. Since (B/r)(t/b)=p, one has

  Z=U xi/(1+xi)+V p/(xi+p).                          (4)

Neither the PSD upper bound on x nor any upper bound on y is used in
the proof. Thus no feasibility claim is made for arbitrary values of
the relaxed variables.

## 3. Consequences if every cap is below one half

If some cap has fraction at least 1/2, (1) is immediate. Suppose henceforth
that all three fractions are strictly below 1/2. Put T=max(U,V),
R=min(U,V), and S=U+V. The two inequalities y+T<k/2 and x+Z<k/2 imply

  x-y>T-R,               x-y<S-2Z.

Consequently Z<R. We now justify the resulting parameter restrictions.
It is harmless algebraically to order U>=V: when swapping them replace
xi by p/xi in (4), which leaves the expression unchanged. Then Z<V and
(4), after subtracting V and dividing by xi>0, give

  U/(1+xi)<V/(xi+p),
  (U-V)xi<V-Up.

Its left side is nonnegative, so V>Up. With V=PQ/U and p=P/Q this is
U<Q. Since V<=U and UV=PQ, we conclude

  0<P<Q,          P<V<=U<Q.                          (5)

Thus the unordered statement is P<R<=T<Q.

## 4. A sharp scalar lower estimate for Z

For every positive xi and 0<P<Q, with V=PQ/U, the exact identity is

  Z-P(2Q-U-V)/(Q-P)
    =[PQ(1+xi)-PU-QU xi]^2
       /[U(Q-P)(P+Q xi)(1+xi)] >=0.                 (6)

This follows by substituting (4) and putting the terms over a common
denominator. Every factor in the denominator is positive. In particular
under (5), Z>=Z_0:=P(2Q-S)/(Q-P)>0. The positivity follows from
S=U+V<Q+P<2Q; the first inequality is equivalent to (Q-U)(Q-V)>0
using UV=PQ.

## 5. Minimize the relaxed largest-cap ratio

For fixed y>0, T,R,Z satisfying Z<R, the function

  max(y+T,x+Z)/(x+y+S)

of x>=0 decreases up to x_0=y+T-Z>0 and increases thereafter.
Before that point its numerator is constant. After that point its
derivative has the positive numerator y+S-Z. Hence for every actual x,

  max_i q_i/k >= (y+T)/(2y+T-Z+S).                  (7)

The derivative of the last expression with respect to y has sign
S-T-Z=R-Z>0. Since y>=Q, (7) gives

  max_i q_i/k >= (Q+T)/(2Q+T-Z+S)
              >= (Q+T)/(2Q+T-Z_0+S).               (8)

The second inequality uses Z>=Z_0; the relevant denominators are
positive. They are positive for the actual Z by their first expression,
and replacing it by a smaller Z_0 only increases the denominator.

Scale all areas by Q, so Q=1. Write P=s^2 with 0<s<1. Then
V=P/U and the ordered variable T lies in [s,1). The final expression
in (8) is

  F_P(T)=(1-P)(1+T)/[2-4P+(2-P)T+P/T].              (9)

Its denominator is positive on this interval. For example,
R-Z_0=P(T-1)^2/[T(1-P)]>0 for T<1, and the denominator before the
positive multiplication by 1-P in (8) is plainly positive.
Direct differentiation gives

  F'_P(T)
    =P(P-1)(T-1)(3T+1)
       /[P T^2+4PT-P-2T^2-2T]^2 >=0.              (10)

Thus F_P(T)>=F_P(s). Substitution and a final exact square yield

  F_(s^2)(s)=(1+s)^2/(s^2+5s+2),
  F_(s^2)(s)-8/17
      =(3s-1)^2/[17(s^2+5s+2)] >=0.                (11)

Combining (7)--(11) proves (1). All variables came from the original
ordinary body; no discarded mixed mass or independent cap tilt enters.

## 6. Consequence for the row-extremum reduction

The independently audited fixed-sector theorem supplies an attained
maximizer of a selected planar row. If its reconstruction is type B,
its opposite singleton nodes and four core sectors meet Section 1.
Its original six sector areas, total area, and cap areas are retained
exactly. Therefore a starting configuration with all cap fractions at
most 128/279 cannot have such a type-B maximizing reconstruction.
The same exclusion holds for any smaller ceiling than 8/17.

The six-vertex type A and all remaining polygons with at most five
vertices are not addressed by this theorem. It neither proves the
ordinary row inequality in those cases nor identifies a mixed center.
